Name: 35_spectrum_5g_network_wireless
Representative_Docs: ["Keep in mind that 5G is not a replacement technology for LTE. LTE will be here for a very long time and be the predominant voice, text, data platform for mobile. So when you look at LTE, currently, what we're doing at [COMPANY] is we are densifying the network. And we're doing that for the densification capacity needs to deliver performance to customers who continue to use LTE. You view that as -- that's a prerequisite to being able to launch 5G at some point down the road. So when you think about small cells, the more small cells you have, the better 5G you will be able to create. Think about that though as we're incurring the capital to install those small cells today to deliver LTE. So when you think about the use case, it's fixed wireless broadband. As far as modeling goes, I think there's 2 hurdles that we still have to get through before we start talking about a wide commercial launch here in the U.S. One is the standards have to be set around 5G. Now we would love to set that standard on a global basis and we're working with South Korea and Japan on trying to establish that, to get that standard set. And the reason you want the standard set is because it makes it much more efficient for everybody to buy the hardware from the manufacturers because they have to -- they only have to build to 1 spec, and that's beneficial to the industry and beneficial to the manufacturer. The second is obviously spectrum because there's no 28 to 39 gigahertz spectrum in large swaths today that's available to be used other than what we actually have an option on, on XO. The FCC has to work with the Department of Justice to free up that spectrum and get it to the marketplace. But that's -- in order to go commercial, we have to have more spectrum than what's there today. So you need to get 28 and 39 because of the millimeter wave and how you deliver the signal.", "I'd like to focus my time today to summarize the key results in fiscal 2018 and to date, specifically through the lens of our focused and executed business strategy and to highlight how this well positions PDV to capture market interest and demand this coming year and into the future. As part of our continued assessment of the landscape of opportunities before us and putting our spectrum to the highest and best use, we identified an important link between the incumbents in our 900 megahertz spectrum band, primarily utilities, some of whom were in opposition and the compelling business opportunity to enable private broadband networks for the same utility industry. So based on this understanding, over the course of the year, we built a lean and experienced team of employees and consultants to lead our commercial outreach to the industry. We then progressed to business development discussions, working intensively with the utility industry's thought leaders and broadband pioneers to design a solution to serve their rapidly growing needs. We came to see that the needs of these utilities boil down to a few common themes, including the desire by large investor-owned utilities or IOUs to own and control their broadband networks as the offerings of commercial carrier networks can't fulfill these fundamental requirements. These utilities also require a solution that provides cost-effective coverage and broadband capacity with reliability, resilience and security that can't be provided under legacy narrowband utility networks. The initial execution of this solutions-based approach to the utility market has yielded substantial gains in our top priorities, both in our regulatory success and in the development of our broadband business. On the regulatory side, utilities and other key players now have a vested interest in seeing our FCC process succeed and have become more vocal of why they want and need the 900 megahertz band to be modernized. And concurrently, we've created much broader industry awareness of our proposed solution, and equally important, we've built a robust pipeline of real commercial demand from utilities for the 900 megahertz broadband spectrum, including the pilots planned for this year. The continued commercial development will allow us to hit the ground running as we emerge from the regulatory process. As a direct result of our commercial progress to date, major utility vendor and industry participants have visited the FCC leadership and expressed urgent need for broadband spectrum in the 900 megahertz band with visits to the commissioners, the Chairman and the Wireless Bureau. It's through this targeted commercial outreach and development with utilities that we've taken a formally lengthy list of opposition that resisted change years ago down to just a few remaining holdouts today. I want to take a minute to highlight some of the representative examples of this specific demand by parties with strong commercial needs that's translated to support at the FCC. Ameren, an industry-leading electric utility, covering 64,000 square miles of Illinois and Missouri joined us to meet with the FCC and stated directly that there's an urgent need for broadband spectrum to solve essential use cases that are required to maintain their ratepayers' quality of life. Ameren also requested that the FCC move quickly to issue a broadband experimental license to allow them to pilot a first-of-its-kind secure 900 megahertz LTE broadband network in both Illinois and Missouri. With fast approval provided by the FCC, Ameren was granted a 2-year experimental license and is currently preparing to launch their multistate pilot program this calendar year, targeted with demonstrating secure, reliable communications to support their grid modernization needs. Ameren currently manages numerous and disparate wireless narrowband networks and an overall goal of this pilot is the long-term consolidation of these networks as well as the support of new additional use cases that can't be solved by existing systems. It's also worth noting that separately with Ameren, we are providing spectrum to support a drone trial being led by Rockwell Collins to demonstrate the ability to serve a utility infrastructure for preventative and restorative maintenance. Southern Company continues to lead the industry innovation for the use of private mission-critical LTE utility needs. In addition to currently deploying the leading edge LTE network in their Alabama and Georgia regions, Southern has also started their strong interest -- stated their strong interest in seeing nationwide proliferation of broadband LTE networks at utilities to drive industry economies of scale, a robust ecosystem of utility applications, device and infrastructure development and to have interoperable systems so that utilities can work together seamlessly when they provide mutual aid in times of crisis, like the unfortunate recent storms and hurricanes we saw this past season. Southern is also providing industry support through their cosponsorship of a supportive resolution at UTC, and we expect more great things as we continue to work with Southern's leadership on advancing 900 megahertz broadband to the industry. Sensus was previously one of the large opponents as they provided advanced metering infrastructure or AMI to utilities to do automatic meter reading for over 14 million meters in the U.S. With the help of our further comments at the FCC addressing their concerns and our friends at Southern Company, Sensus' largest customer, we were able to reach an agreement with Sensus that led to a turnaround in their position, resulting in their recent filed support at the FCC. Several other Sensus users were previously opposed, and we are optimistic that the Sensus support will now bring them around as well. We also have several strong examples of utilities with incumbent 900 megahertz narrowband systems that are supportively working with us to retune their systems in advance of any rulemaking. SMUD, a community-owned electric utility in Sacramento, California, serving 1.4 million people, has also worked in advance with PDV to retune their systems and explained in their FCC comments that the realignment proposal is a reasonable approach and has quoted the realignment of a 900 megahertz spectrum has the potential to provide the broadband that SMUD and the electric utilities need. They filed support for the reconfiguration of the 900 megahertz band to provide broadband licensing, stating that their long-term projections to 2023 determined that they would be requiring 5 megabits per second to each endpoint due in part to the increased cybersecurity requirements of the North American Energy Reliability Corporation (sic) [ North American Electric Reliability Corporation ] or NERC. And as a sample of the vendor support, Ericsson, a global leader in broadband LTE systems, has filed strongly supportive comments and has been into the FCC to express the urgent need that they are seeing for this broadband spectrum from utility customers. Lastly, industry leaders like [PERSON] and General Dynamics have stated their strong support for the FCC proceeding and that they see compelling needs for private broadband networks in other complementary segments of users, including enterprise and government. Switching to PDV's second key priority, building a robust broadband business opportunity. We're working with -- both directly with utilities and leading global LTE infrastructure vendors, including Ericsson and Nokia, to address the pent-up needs of their customers for private broadband LTE solutions. To paint the picture of the driving forces that are causing the increased market demand for private broadband networks utilities, I'll share with you some background. To successfully meet the reliability and resiliency demands of the critical systems, private broadband networks built on licensed spectrum are being sought to secure the robust communications infrastructure needed for these advanced technologies. And in Navigant Research's recent white paper entitled The Urgent Need for a Licensed Broadband Spectrum Allocation for Critical Infrastructure, the point is made that the utility practice of managing dozens of unlicensed narrowband wireless networks is uneconomical and presents a multitude of risks to grid performance and operational security, an alternative strategy must be found. PDV's 900 megahertz provides superior coverage and penetration characteristics of a sub-1 gigahertz spectrum band, with existing off-the-shelf LTE technology and devices that allow for a foundation of cost-effective coverage for private wireless systems. As we continue to consciously deploy our limited capital on the heightened focus on the future broadband opportunities as I just highlighted, we've come to a clear inflection point in our business. Our determination to make this change is heavily supported by our increasing confidence in the prospects of our broadband business and our desire to shift our investment and focus to this area of targeted higher returns for our shareholders. We continue to focus our investment dollars towards the best opportunities that have the most promising and positive impact on shareholder value. In this coming year, we're focusing on achieving the key elements of success that will be the catalyst in realizing our strategic plan. These include effectively managing our resources, both money and people, to drive the continued growth of commercial opportunities, turning our spectrum into customer solutions, feeding into the advancement of our FCC agenda. Our goal of these commercial offerings will be long-term relationships with high valuable -- highly valuable, high credit customers that translate into substantial value for our shareholders. To think that less than 4 years ago, when we embarked on this journey to build a private broadband network, most industry participants did not know what this meant. And here we are today, and what was once a concept is now a reality, with the broader industry attesting to the growing need for such networks. The confluence of current events with utilities at the epicenter led by grid modernization and distributed generation in virtually every state as well as the risks to cybersecurity is driving the demand for private broadband networks. This demand is met with the supply of robust off-the-shelf private LTE solutions from leading global vendors that are now being designed to be scaled and tailored to the needs of the regional utility footprints.", "So the 900 megahertz band is part of the 3GPP standard and will evolve into 5G as well. And so initially, the FCC has granted 6 megahertz of spectrum, which there are efforts within 3GPP to have that defined and evolve into a 5G standard. Eventually, we think there's an opportunity to -- whether it's through spectrum consolidation in other bands, in conjunction with CBRS or other bands, we think there's opportunity for -- we used to call that in the carrier days a rich man's problem, right? If you've used up all your capacity, it means you're fully getting the value of that particular spectrum and you can justify either purchasing or acquiring other spectrum as well. So we see that 900 megahertz will be part of the 5G standard as it evolves. Utilities are not known to be bleeding-edge technology users. And so as that becomes the standard, I'm certain that, that will evolve to their needs as well."]

Name: 36_railroad_intermodal_train_rail
Representative_Docs: ["So to your point, I came to CP with a mandate to change: change the operation; fix the engine. At the same time though, we got the engine so to speak to a point from a service level, from productivity, whether you look at train links, train weights, fuel efficiencies, all sort of the levers that drive the big cost buckets in our business, as well as the service offering we give the customer. I think Canada benefits from the 2 best-run railways in the industry. If you look at the service metrics, you look at the operating metrics, you look at our cost control, but more specifically, CP now, the next part of the story is to grow the top line even more. We had service-sensitive customers, domestic, intermodal, that's an area that we've grown -- driven some growth over the past 3 years. So what we started to do and focus on, is how do we convert service to growth? Number one, you got to get reliability; you got to get credibility. And while you do that, as you establish reliability and credibility with the customer, you do it by turning assets. So we've driven dramatic growth on the domestic side. Last year, in a down market, we were the only railway in North America -- the only railway in North America that drove positive intermodal growth and it was driven by domestic growth, which depends upon service. There's still a tremendous amount of run room, so to speak, and it's more not focused on taking share from my rail competitors, it's focused on taking share off the road. Well, it's big, but again, you got to have truck-like service offering. You got to be reliable, and you got to be transit time competitive. With the strength of our network, we are shorter in the key routes in domestic intermodal. In Canada, it gives us an ability to go out and sell a product that is unique in the industry. They're an extension of our railway, an extension of our sales force and that's what's driving growth. So that's a key area of growth for us as we go forward. To really understand Intermodal business, International Intermodal the margins are low, domestic it's much more service sensitive so the customers are willing to pay for it. And, again, compared to domestic versus international, the margins and the sustainability is a lot more attractive in the international business is, and we control the terminals, we control the product, from picking it up it to delivering which is positive. The other piece that's super positive for this franchise and our story is now that we've got service reliability and low cost, we're going to grow the merchandise business. That 35% merchandise -- we're in a position now, again, think about what drives strength to franchise and service offering on Domestic Intermodal is our franchise footprint. So when those markets -- again, if you've got customers that never could depend upon your service -- merchandise customers that run assembly lines in Canada that might take a product, say, from Edmonton to Vancouver or Edmonton to Toronto to run that facility, they couldn't trust us in the past because we'd shut the assembly lines down. Now we can compete. If you can't go in and tell a customer, how you can save them money and they still give you a fair rate for your transportation by selling service then you're in your wrong business, that's compelling. Those stories were just starting to be able to happen because, again, we had to establish that credibility. On the growth and the top line, I'm focused on this railroad. There's to $200 million to $300 million of that kind of business as these contracts come open and as these doors get open and as the sales force gets more disciplined and they have the same kind of culture in the sales force that we have in the operating side. It's extremely powerful, it'll allow us to repatriate that business and grow the top line and drive very meaningful earnings growth as we go forward.", "I've always been a proponent personally, until and unless we get the components that we put our trains together with to become more reliable. There's just -- when you put a train together, there's a lot of moving parts and those moving parts historically have created some challenges. We should not be put in a disadvantaged place when technology allows safe and efficient operation, components allow safe and efficient operation to be disadvantaged from realizing the benefits of that and staying competitive. And that to me is exactly what that smells of to put us in a place where all those things being accomplished, we're at a disadvantage a cost disadvantage. We're not able to do our very dead level best to take trucks off the road, put them on the rail to allow the customers to enjoy the benefits of those cost synergies as well as the environment enjoy the benefits of those less greenhouse gas emissions. We're talking about reducing greenhouse gas emissions, but yet, we're talking and looking at potential actions by the regulator that says we can't do that or we can't optimize that outcome. I just hope that as the discussions evolve around this topic that we really think about the unintended consequences and think about the totality of what's being suggested. So it's not just as simple as implementing and integrating in different railroads have had various levels of success. I can say that this pandemic and this manpower issue, if you don't have people, trains don't move. And some things have occurred in the middle of PSR implementation they, quite frankly, stack the deck against these other railroads. If you're sitting outside of a terminal and you can't get in the terminal because the train is too large, there are unintended consequences. If you're doubling trains out of terminals and parking them on main lines, waiting on power because you're holding out one of those big trains because it can't get in the terminal, you have unintended consequences. I know that, obviously, it's affected the railroads overall ability to serve customers' needs, but I do see it getting better. I see getting to a place that is these railroads get their cadence and the rhythm and they get more experience in muscle memory in these processes that it takes to actually effectively run a PSR railroad, I think it's the right way to run a business. But we learn from those, we bake those into the way railroad today, and I think you can produce a better outcome. We've grown like not the railroad has over the last for 5 years, and we've created an infrastructure and a rhythm and an ability and respect with our customers and our trust with our customers that we're helping them win in their marketplaces as we win for all stakeholders, and we're doing it as a PSR railroad. And I think eventually, the industry will get there as well. And the best thing we can do is continue to improve. The best thing I can do, and we can do at CP is make sure that our story, our unique story and our unique outcome running a PSR operating model is understood, and that's exactly what we're committed to doing.", "They're going to try to get standardized, higher capacity, more efficient equipment in their fleet. That's a tactical thing, it can affect us, for example, because we compete aggressively in that market. So homogenization is difficult to achieve in the rail industry and they always strive for it. But the rail lever there would be moving to higher capacity cars. So what happens when you're talking about a more efficient railroad, you're talking about longer moves, block moves, and sometimes train schedules that are really for the convenience of the railroads as opposed to the convenience of the shipper. If they have deteriorating service by concentrating trains and they have difficulty with feeder systems to get that concentration, it actually can be negative for the railroad. So we're all living in this world of railroading where operating ratio is everything. I think that even [PERSON], as much as he did, because he's actually seen the consequences of attempting to do it, put on the heat. If customers are not happy, they're going to try to find an alternative. So we want railroad remain competitive as a shipping mode, so steps like precision railroading to the degree to be successful are not concerning to us if they succeed. The customer creates all the value. Why do railroads or shippers need cars to move freight? So there's a limit to how much pricing and how much service deterioration you can have."]

Name: 37_tenants_retailers_retail_shopping
Representative_Docs: ["The core asset type for the combined company, that's one of the great attributes of the deal that we mentioned earlier is that both companies own very, very high quality Class A real estate. And it's predominantly large -- what we call, large power centers or community shopping centers who are anchored by national tenants, and also shadow-anchored by national tenants. So I would say that the majority of the assets owned by the combined company are those type of very powerful regional shopping centers that are close to 200,000 square feet on average,, made up of absolutely outstanding national tenants, complemented by smaller national and regional and local tenants. So -- in addition to that, the combined company will own a significant amount of grocery-anchored shopping centers that are smaller-format centers, but outstanding shopping centers and strong real estate. So that's definitely one of the biggest attributes of this transaction, is that both companies own very good portfolios, which we now have an even better portfolio in the combination.", "Last year, we had a busy and productive quarter, both on the investment front where we completed over $1 billion of transactions, as well as with respect to our existing assets, where leasing and redevelopment activity continues to create an important long-term growth. 6 years ago, we announced that we were refocusing our core acquisition activities towards building a differentiated and forward-looking portfolio with a meaningful concentration of assets in our nation's most dynamic, urban and street retail corridors. And this has been in response to the changes, both in retailer demand as retailers are adapting their business to the ongoing evolution of omni-channel retailing as well as the many different consumer trends. All in all, these changes are resulting in a growing separation between the have and have-not locations in retail real estate. And it's pretty clear to us that retailers will continue shedding more generic locations and continue to focus on mission-critical locations. In all instances, it's imperative that we remain disciplined in our investing. That has enabled us to avoid some of the pain that others are experiencing today. It's also positioning us for some interesting future investment opportunities. But most importantly is to not lose sight of the fact that this temporary overcrowding of the street retail trade in 2015 does not contradict the long-term trend of how our retailers are refining their fleets. In fact, the trend is playing out more or less as retailers have forecasted. And location matters today, more than it ever has. And while it's frustrating to watch some of our traditional retailers struggle through this transition, I'm confident that many of them will succeed and it's also exciting to see some of our newer online-first retailers moving from screens to stores as they recognize the importance of having strong bricks and mortar presence as well. Our thesis has been that over the long term, these types of properties should generate NOI growth that is superior to our suburban assets by at least 200 basis points. This is driven roughly in equal parts by stronger contractual growth and stronger market growth with more frequent mark-to-market opportunities due to fair market value, option resets, recapture and retenanting activities. As [PERSON] will discuss our fourth quarter results as well as our full year 2016 performance, we're consistent with this thesis as is our leasing and redevelopment activities in 2017 where we are successfully recapturing a handful of locations and will profitably release them. And although the short-term disruption in rent will weigh on our 2017 metrics, as [PERSON] will discuss, the value created by these [indiscernible] will be meaningful and visible in 2018 and beyond. And as we look beyond the next 12 to 24 months, the growth looks even more compelling. Over the next 5 years, nearly half of our urban and street retail NOI is projected to grow by an incremental $11 million to $12 million of NOI, growing from $36 million to $48 million. And this growth should thus help drive the growth for our overall core portfolio. First, let me touch on the 2016 acquisitions. The acquisitions are comprised of approximately 70% street retail, 30% urban. And while it's easy to see that these assets provide strong downside protection due to their tenancy and in-demand locations, as importantly, they also have strong embedded growth primarily driven by lease-up in the portfolio where we should be able to take the economic occupancy from its current 91%, up to our more historic average of 95%. The other half of the growth comes from the leasing and redevelopment of opportunities in 7 of our existing urban and street retail properties. Beginning in 2017 and over the next 5 years, we anticipate harvesting about $5.5 million of incremental NOI. In January, we executed a new lease with lululemon for their Rush Street store in Chicago's Gold Coast where they'll turn their existing store with us into a flagship location by taking over part of an adjacent building that we own. At a time when many retailers are being forced to learn to do more with less, we're also seeing, in certain critical locations, select retailers recognizing the importance of also doing more with more. A second driver of this growth is in connection with our Lincoln Park Chicago redevelopment located at Clark and Diversey. Other retailers at our property here include Trader Joe's, Urban Outfitters and Starbucks. Then in Washington, D.C., we successfully recaptured a building formerly leased to Lacoste on M Street and Georgetown, and we have released that at a 50% leasing spread. So as it relates to our core portfolio, our 2016 acquisitions and our 7 embedded value opportunities, which again represent just under half of our urban and street retail NOI, should be important drivers in generating above-average growth over the next several years, as I've just outlined. And we also expect that from time to time, the other half of our urban and street retail portfolio will also have outsized growth opportunities as we get closer to more mark-to-market opportunities there. As [PERSON] will discuss, this has created increased opportunities to deploy capital through our fund platform at attractive leverage returns. Our core assets are poised for long-term growth as we continue to navigate a shifting retail landscape. Our balance sheet is fully reloaded, giving us transactional flexibility.", 'And I think if you look around our neighborhood and community shopping center sector, also euphemistically called the open air center, the industry is very healthy today. Occupancy is up. Rents are going up. Leasing spreads are very positive. Renewals are strong. So what we call the vital signs or the fundamentals of the shopping center industry are very good today. And I think that\'s across the industry and you see it in the metrics. And there are several reasons for that. Number one is there\'s virtually no new building activity. Secondly, the U.S. continues to have excellent population growth of close to 3 million people a year, and the economy is finally doing better with strong positive GDP. So you put those 3 things in the hopper, and it\'s really helped the shopping center industry. Let me finish on this slide by talking about our balance sheet, which is one of the strongest in the industry. We\'re one of only 14 REITs that have a rating from all 3 rating agencies, a BBB or effectively BBB+. So we\'re in the top 10% of all REITs in terms of balance sheet strength. The returns, since our IPO in 1991, have been very strong. If you compare [COMPANY] versus the Dow Jones and the S&P 500, you\'ll see that we\'ve outperformed both since our IPO and over a 5-year period, so we\'re proud of that. If you look at some highlights, we do have our very long, long history in this shopping center space. [PERSON], the founder of [COMPANY], started developing shopping centers in Florida in 1957, and he knows every single asset that he developed and we have most of them still in the portfolio. We have a national platform, which gives us certain -- I don\'t want to say leverage, but ability to form relationships with retailers. Because we\'re in just about every market in the United States, retailers, national retailers are happy to meet with us because they have a way to expand geographically across the country rather than meeting with somebody that\'s more regionally focused. We have a combination of what you would call grocery-anchored shopping centers and food-anchored properties, and what they call power centers or big-box centers where we\'re about 50-50. Pure grocery-anchored is probably about 1/3 of the portfolio. And if you add Costcos and Walmart Supercenters and others that anchor some of our shopping centers, you get up to almost 60% of our portfolio is food anchored in some form or fashion. What sets us out a little bit from others, we have what we have called the "PLUS" business. But essentially, we have for many, many years invested opportunistically in real estate that\'s owned by distressed retailers. So as an example, when Montgomery Ward went out of business in the early 2000s, [COMPANY], together with GE, purchased all of the Montgomery Ward real estate and found homes for that real estate. 50 of them went to Target, and others went to others. But it\'s an example of where we opportunistically invested. In more recent years, we bought Albertsons. Last year, we invested in 5 brands owned by SUPERVALU, which included Star Market, Shaw\'s, Jewel, ACME and the remaining portion of Albertsons. And it was announced earlier this year that we are now going to combine with Safeway, so that large merger is with the FTC right now. But overall, it\'s a small part of our business, but it is an opportunistic part of our business and we make quite a bit of money in that business. This slide is a little better at illustrating the point I was trying to make in terms of the new supply of shopping centers in our space is at historically low levels. This is a country that, at its peak, was building 2,000 shopping centers a year. We\'re down to less than 100. So even if you double or triple that number, the supply side of the equation remains very, very subdued. The appetite for developers to buy large tracts of land, go through 5 years of zoning and entitlement battles and then pre-lease and get construction financing, equity financing is very limited. So the supply side of our business is very limited and very helpful in terms of helping us recover rents and so forth. On the demand side of the equation, you have almost 77,000 new stores that will be opened up over the next 2 years, which is close to a 5-year high in terms of the demand side of the equation. All kinds of national retailers are expanding. So there are certain industries that are growing like crazy. There\'s a restaurant category called fast casual, Panera Bread, Chipotle and others. [COMPANY]\'s strategy is relatively simple. Like many of our peers, we\'re spending time upgrading our portfolio. We\'re selling the bottom tier of our portfolio, the properties that are in secondary and tertiary markets or that are secondary properties themselves. And we\'re reinvesting those proceeds either in redeveloping our better properties or buying better properties. We are also spending an awful lot of time, what we call is in developing the redevelopment pipeline. Our redevelopment pipeline today is up to $1 billion of projects that we have. Over the years, we\'ve also simplified in the sense that we\'re largely exiting Latin America. The investment community never gave us much credit for being in South America and Mexico. And so today, we\'re focusing primarily on the U.S. and Canada, both strong long-term markets for us. Diversification is probably a strength of the company. We have basically 13,000 leases with 6,500 individual tenants spread over those 840 properties. So -- and there\'s no tenant that provides more than 3% or significantly more than 3% of our gross revenues. So there\'s definitely a wonderful spread of risk and a diversification to our income stream. As part of our simplification strategy where we\'ve identified about 15 core primary markets where we believe there\'s going to be excellent job growth, excellent population growth, where the top retailers want to be, where they\'re opening new stores, where income levels are getting higher and so forth, and this map illustrates. But as an example, things like Florida, Texas, California are pretty obvious. But others like Denver and Seattle, Portland, North Carolina we like a lot, Raleigh, Charlotte area. So this map demonstrates some of these core markets for us, but still gives us a very national footprint. This next slide gives you again a picture of how our portfolio breaks down between small shops, mom and pops, if you will, and larger anchor tenants like Home Depot and Walmart. But you\'ll see the portfolio again, there\'s a nice spread between the small shops which are generally shorter leases but higher rent leases, and anchor tenants which are longer-term leases but generally lower rents. We would argue because we are neighborhood and community-focused shopping centers where our retailers are selling essential goods and services with a huge service component. So the Internet, which has increased their market share in retail sales over time, is not quite as a danger to the local neighborhood shopping center as perhaps other types of retail. In a broader way, most brick-and-mortar retailers have found a way to adapt and evolve their own online and e-commerce strategy. So for various reasons, whether it\'s a showroom or a fulfillment center or a way to get returns from Internet sales, brick-and-mortar stores are very important to e-commerce sales. This is a chart that shows you the metrics that I mentioned before, are all getting stronger over time, as we recover from the Great Recession. I think the most -- the critical thing for me is that rents in the neighborhood and community shopping center space still haven\'t recovered to where they were in 2007, 2008. So there\'s room for rents to continue to go up, especially because supply is so limited. But suffice it to say, what we\'re buying today are in these primary markets where we think there\'s excellent job growth and where the retailers want to be. What we\'re selling are demographic areas that we think are a little bit challenged in terms of long-term future population growth, job growth and so forth. And that\'s upgraded our portfolio, helped make us a much higher-quality portfolio. In terms of simplification, those of you that don\'t know [COMPANY], we have a very large asset management platform. We manage about $10 billion of shopping centers for other institutions: Pension funds, life insurance companies, Canada Pension Plan, other GE Pension Trust, people like that. And over time, over the last couple of years, we\'ve reduced the number of these joint ventures and simplified the business model. It\'s also been an excellent opportunity for us to buy a 100% interest in a joint venture where we may have owned 50%. And because in many cases, these institutions have decided to reinvest their capital in other areas or they\'ve made a lot of money in a venture with us, we\'ve been able to buy them out at what we think are attractive prices. So this slide illustrates how at one time, our peak, we had more than 550 properties in joint ventures, and that\'s now down to 377 and should fall further. This is a picture of one, the before and after picture. Generally, we target at least a 10% return on the incremental capital we\'ve invested. But in general, it\'s probably the most attractive place for us to put capital today, back into our own property. So we\'re working very hard to increase the number of redevelopments in our pipeline. The balance sheet, as I mentioned before, is very strong. And like most public companies, we\'ve been trying to take advantage of this historic low interest rate market. So when you\'re able to access long-term debt at those kinds of numbers, it improves the earnings profile of the company. We also pushed out our line of credit. Our net debt-to-EBITDA, which is what the rating agencies look at when they establish the ratings, is now down to about 5.7%, something like that. And our targeted range is 5.5% to 6%, with a fixed charge coverage of 2.5%, which is another key metric the rating agencies look at. Again, this just gives you some gross asset numbers. Our dividend payout ratio is one of the lowest in the REIT world. So it gives you 2 things: One, it gives you an ability to raise the dividend comfortable, or it gives you a cushion in bad times. This shows you the growth of our recurring retail earnings. This is the rents coming from our shopping center portfolio. And so it gives our investors and our company comfort that we can deliver the dividend, and increase it on a reliable consistent basis. We are the largest, and we\'ve been around just about the longest period of time with over 50 years of history and experience. Our balance sheet is exceptionally strong. We have an embedded pipeline of this redevelopment and ways to create value in our own portfolio because it is large. And as we\'ve said again, we\'re a proven opportunistic investor when the right opportunities present themselves.']

Name: 38_oncology_pipeline_development_therapeutic
Representative_Docs: ["I've seen incredible growth in this business over the past 12 years but I truly feel our best days are ahead of us. My goal during the presentation is to help you understand how our unique business model can compound growth over time and drive significant long-term stakeholder value. One, we're experiencing continued momentum in our business. Two, we have a long track record of successful capital deployment. We built a highly fruitful diversified portfolio that provides low-risk access to 35 commercial products, including 12 blockbusters, many of the products in our portfolio are in the early years of their launches with substantial growth ahead of them. Three, we're leveraging a highly efficient, diversified business model with among the lowest cost of capital in the industry to drive future growth. Fourth and finally, we're so confident in the opportunity today ahead of us that we can say with confidence that we expect to generate top line growth of 10% or more over this decade. We collect royalties on market-leading products across the biopharma industry, which drives adjusted cash receipts or our top line. The vast majority of our remaining cash flow gets redeployed into new long-duration royalties at attractive rates of return. The process of identifying new royalties, conducting due diligence and structuring deals is extremely complex. [PERSON] has a proven track record of compounding growth. We're a fairly new public company, but the growth profile we're describing today is not new. We expect [PERSON] to grow over the long term, irrespective of individual royalty expiries. [PERSON] has a strong track record of continuously refreshing our portfolio with market-leading therapies. Our growth outlook has evolved nicely over time, and well ahead of our initial guidance at IPO. Today, we're now targeting 11% to 14% through 2025, which is nearly a 50% increase at the midpoint of our guidance. First, our existing portfolio has performed well. And second, our powerful model is working. So as I just covered, we used cash flow and conservative leverage to buy value-enhancing royalties, and this leads to attractive compounding long-term growth. We're really proud of the scale of capital deployment. We've always believed our growth stands out for 3 reasons. The first is the diversity of growth. At 11% to 14%, we think our growth compares really well across biopharma, but really all industries. Around 90% of our deals over the last 2 years have durations beyond 2030. Capital deployment is a key metric for our business. But over the long term, we see an opportunity to double this capital deployment to $4 billion to $5 billion per year. An important benefit of our portfolio is that we're diversified across products, therapeutic areas and marketers. These were products approved prior to 2018. We expect this segment of the portfolio to have a CAGR of 3% in 2020 to 2025. We expect the segment of the portfolio to grow at a CAGR of around 70% over the period from very little in 2020 and to $350 million to $450 million by 2025. Representative_Docs: ["So we start with the largest -- in fact, it is the largest fiber network, 1 million-plus route mile of fiber is what [COMPANY] owns as part of our fiber asset. Either the assets we have or assets that we find ways through different arrangements, different partners we go acquire, but we start from a position of strength with where we're at. The key with fiber is how you actually deploy it. So from an engineering principle, integrating all of your needs as you build fiber is absolutely critical. We take the collective needs of [COMPANY] and our collective businesses. What businesses do we want to sell fiber services into? What residential areas or consumer areas do we want to offer broadband that gigabit speed into? Where do we find a need for small cells in the future? Bringing all of those aspects together is the way that we build a fiber plan because the person that's planning that fiber, the most important thing they need to know is the total needs for the area, so they know how many fibers to put in the cable. And so why that's important is the cost of a fiber build is not the fiber itself, but the placing cost, the build cost, down streets and down alleyways and through backyards, that's where the cost is. And so the economics of fiber are that as you build deeper, the next need is incrementally cheaper and quicker to do. Because that business that I wanted to offer fiber services to, that might be 1,000 feet away today, when I do that job for a residential or broadband consumer capability, maybe I'm only 500 feet away from that business now. Highlights of the previously announced Phase 1 of the Palms redevelopment include a complete renovation of the casino floor, with an expanded number of table games and upgraded slot product as well as an additional new high-limit room at both -- for both slots and table games; our vibrant new Lucky Penny Café, which opened in July to stellar reviews; an all new take on the all-you-can-eat buffet concept, which is currently scheduled to open this December; a new stylish and sophisticated steakhouse that will reset the standard for Las Vegas steakhouses; an intimate and authentic noodle bar restaurant; a new rooftop social club offered by Clique Hospitality Group, a leader in Las Vegas nightlife, which will offer unparalleled views of the city; an exclusive high-end casino lounge experience also managed by Clique Hospitality Group; a new iconic center bar; 18,000 net square feet of completely renovated meeting and convention space; a new hotel front-desk registration and VIP registration reception areas; a fully upgraded 14-screen movieplex featuring luxury recliner tiered stadium seating in every theater; and an all new exterior look, including a new marquee, modernized product, porte-cochère and new exterior facades and lush landscaping. As you can see, this transformation will touch virtually every aspect of the property and, once complete, we're confident the Palms will become the ultimate gaming and entertainment destination for both locals and tourists alike.", "As [PERSON] mentioned, we are best-in-market operators, not only here in Las Vegas, but in Detroit and in Mississippi. But today, we're going to focus our discussion mainly on Las Vegas, and mainly because we believe Las Vegas is well positioned to outperform in the next several years. Name: 52_biotech_pharma_discovery_biopharma
Representative_Docs: ["So we are a leading drug discovery company. We pride ourselves in having a unique portfolio of products and services. Our client makeup has shifted appropriately. And for the last 2013 and through this year, biotech companies represent more of our revenue than our Big Pharma clients, and that's a change for us. And that's, I think, an appropriate change given the amounts of drugs that are coming out of biotech. Asia Pacific is growing, as our Chinese business grows. Breakdown of our segments is actually quite interesting. Business is quite profitable, typically in the high 20s. Discovery and Safety Assessment is also about 40% of our revenue, so Research Models and Services with DSA are about the same size these days. The profitability of that business is lower but improving, and that represents about 28% of our operating income. And our Manufacturing Support business is a little less than 20% of our revenue but almost 30% of our operating income, high-growth, high-margin business. And we've broken out EMD here, which is a very important business, which is our highest-growth business. Discovery Services business, which is one of the businesses we're really focusing on from a growth point of view and from an interface with our pharma clients and biotech clients in different ways than we have historically, is growing nicely. And we find ourselves in a go and no-go business increasingly, and we're now able to help the clients discern whether to continue to develop their drugs very early on in the process, often before the drug goes to the animals and every stepping-off point along the way as to whether or not they actually want to move into a regulated trial. So for the drug companies, it's very important to spend the money where they have the highest probability of success of getting drugs into the market; and conversely, to stop investing in drugs that don't look promising. Without overstating it, in large measure, they kind of changed the game deal for us in as much as it opens up a whole large opportunity, interface with clients in the discovery area, which is probably $6 billion to $8 billion market, larger than the toxicology market. And we really have been focused on moving upstream. And the opportunities for larger, more interesting and complex deals with our clients is definitely derived specifically from these expanded portfolios. So our goal has been to engage with the clients as early as possible and help them with these go and no-go decisions, as I said before. So the combination of our Argenta, BioFocus and ChanTest has expanded our capabilities dramatically and continue to provide a very solid foundation for us to do further M&A as well as internal investment in the discovery space. We continue to be a leader in that field, both in terms of non-GLP studies, general toxicology and very much so in specialty tox, in areas like infusion tox, bone tox, ocular tox, immunotox and phototox. We're continuing to sign larger and larger deals with both Big Pharma, big and small biotech. Biologics Testing is a business that we've been in for a while, but it's really come of age over the last 12 to 18 months. And obviously, as more and more drugs get into the clinic and get to market, which are large molecule based, this business will be more relevant and more important and we should see it be an increasingly larger product at [COMPANY]. Our Endotoxin, Microbial Detection business continues to be our fastest-growing business. So we're the only people now that can do both endotoxin and bioburden, and we think this is a very large opportunity for us. So as we watch the changes in the pharmaceutical industry, as they have pared down numbers of therapeutic areas, as they've really rationalized their pipelines, as they have sought to have a smaller number of research partners, as they have become increasingly more comfortable and confident and reliant on outsourcing, we have seen virtually all of our Big Pharma clients and all of our big biotech clients embrace some form of outsourcing. But we think that, that's inevitable that the types of work that we do for them, which we can do as well or better, as fast or faster and typically for a better value proposition for them, that these relationships will continue to build. So we're really enjoying the sort of evolution of the drug industry and the sort of crossover between the services we can provide and the services that they need. So what has become clear to us that strategic relationships are critically important to the growth and development and strength of [COMPANY]. We want to get on the same side of the table as our clients. They're all different. Now what's become abundantly clear to us in the last few years is that while the pharmaceutical industry is very interested in working with as many collaborators as possible, including other drug companies and biotech, NGOs and academics and venture firms, so we're establishing strategic relationships with all of these groups. We have several direct investment relationships with venture capital firms, which are allowing us to work closely with a portfolio of companies, particularly their start-up virtual companies. We have more than 25% of our total revenue across all of our product and service lines related to these large corporate deals, and we have several conversations ongoing right now to expand current deals and also to initiate new ones. Growth rate for the biotech sector has been the strongest. And that makes a lot of sense as the biotech companies have become and increasingly become the discovery engines for the pharmaceutical industry. And very focused on our R&D efforts. They're very focused on the science and speed to market. We're also spending a lot of time trying to sell more effectively into the academic institutions. We have grown our academic revenue substantially and intend to continue to focus on that. I would say over the last 3 or 4 years, we have -- we've become very focused on driving efficiency and productivity in the company. So from a strategic point of view, we're looking to drive our top line through strategic acquisitions that grow the portfolio and are accretive; continued internal investment in our businesses, all of them, particularly our growth business. For us, it's all about share gains. We're going to continue to try to expand our current strategic relationships and initiate new ones, both with large pharma, small pharma and large and small biotech and hopefully, increasingly with our academic colleagues. And we believe our portfolio is as strong as it's ever been. We believe that it's stronger than any of our competitors, and we will continue to strengthen that portfolio and broaden it through additional M&A activities and through direct investments.", "Okay, so we're engaged with the drug industry, large and small companies from very early in the discovery process all the way through to drugs being approved. We have an integrated unique portfolio of products and services, increasingly services that we -- have become a significant competitive advantage for us, done 6 acquisitions in the last 24 months, 3 last year. So we continue to expand this portfolio. It's all early -- it's all nonclinical but relatively early in the drug discovery and development process and tends to keep us with the clients throughout the whole process. Client base has shifted a bit but half -- over half of our sales to the biotech companies and other would include chemical companies, other CROs, for instance. I think that since biotech is principally a U.S. phenomenon, and we should expect to see those numbers stay the same or perhaps North America be even increase further. We've also have a -- had a very robust year in our GEMS businesses, that's Genetically Engineered Models, so those are animal models which have either had genes knocked in or knocked out, so they express certain disease states. These models are becoming increasingly more important in translational medicine, when you want to predict how a drug will work in people, you make an animal model that somehow represents the human form of the disease as closely as possible. We're very -- we're interested in signing with the clients as early as possible in drug development process and we moved into the what I would call the go and no-go business and we are helping clients discern as early as possible, whether the drugs are likely to be successful and they should continue to invest aggressively in them or conversely, they just don't look like they're ever going to make it. So Discovery business, we think it will be a high-growth business for us, all through M&As so far. So if you look at the trends with our client base, you'll see that the global pharma clients are reducing their infrastructure dramatically in favor of more outsourcing, so many of the things that we do, our clients used to do exclusively for themselves, we're seeing some consolidation by Big Pharma with one another, although we haven't seen one of those deals in a few years, it was a couple rumored, now and -- but we've also seen the big drug companies buying more biotech. Biotech companies are -- they are accelerating in terms of the quality and types of science so we're seeing all the immunos, as I said earlier, all the immuno-oncology, we're seeing monoclonal antibodies work, we're also seeing residual -- we're seeing RNAi, so you're turning on and off genes, we're seeing gene editing which is exactly that we're seeing proteomics, so all of these technologies that have been developed, being developed for a number of years are actually beginning to work now. So the issue is who are they going to outsource it to, and who will they stay with during the development of their molecule, so our growth has been largely driven by the biotech sector over the last 2 or 3 years. Academic institutions are increasingly being more involved in drug discovery and development, mostly discovery. So seeing sort of 4 different client bases, and I would say over the last few years for the first time in the history of the drug industry, we're seeing an enormous amount of collaboration. It's clear that no specific segment can do this on their own, so we're seeing pharma work with biotech, we're seeing biotech work with the NGOs, we're seeing pharma work with academic institutions. Not to overstate our importance but we're often the interface of pharma with biotech or pharma with the academic institutions so collaboration is very, very powerful for this industry. So just to quickly look at our segments, we have 3, Discovery and Safety Assessment, which is about half of our revenue, plus 42% of our operating income, our operating margins were in the low 20s last year. We have an emerging demand from large biopharma to work with the discovery companies. Our Safety Assessment business, our toxicology business, where we made an acquisition this past year, we have a very good capacity utilization at the current time, we're opening small amounts of space slightly ahead of when we need it and we're hiring hundreds of people in this business to accommodate the work. High growth in China right now, very nascent market, it's going to be perhaps as big as the U.S. We're building additional facilities in that marketplace also very high growth in our Genetically Engineered Models business. This business has been overly manual in a lot of ways, and we've put in some IT systems that are driving efficiency, better utilization of capacity and better inventory management so we're seeing the margins improve nicely here. And our last segment is Manufacturing Support, most profitable part of our business, where we've got revenue growing slightly higher than 20% and profits in the high 20s. This is mostly manufacturing QC testing business, I talked about microbial solutions and biologics, our long-term growth rate for this business are low double digit organic growth and low 30% operating margins which we're actually already achieving in this segment. The portfolio continues to expand, as I said earlier, we think that through additional M&A, which is the #1 use of our capital, we'll continue to expand the portfolio. We're looking at any of the businesses in which we have high-growth metrics, particularly in Discovery and Safety. Increasingly, I would, our say our relationships with our clients is strategic in nature. We are coming up with very tailored solutions, particularly the small biotech companies who want very creative deals, often milestone deals. We're obviously investing in the areas where we have the best possible growth rates. We did it in 6, so we're now down to about 2.7 turns, so we're feeling quite that -- we'll be quite able to financially afford additional M&A. \r\nWe like deals that are $100 million and $200 million in revenue. And we're focusing on several of those. So terrific '16, very optimistic about '17, going to continue to build out our portfolio which provides a distinct competitive advantage, and we have to breakout where?", "I'd like to begin by providing a summary of our outstanding third quarter results before commenting on our business prospects. The acquisitions of ChanTest, Sunrise, and Celsis contributed 3.3% to year-over-year revenue growth, however, Safety Assessment was the primary driver of the robust third quarter results, outperforming our high expectations. In addition, many of our businesses reported higher constant currency revenue than in the third quarter of last year. We were particularly pleased that sales of research models increased in every geographic region except Japan, where pharma industry consolidation has continued to impact sales. All 3 business segments reported increased operating margins, driven by either higher revenue, or improved operating efficiency, or both. We were extremely pleased with the third quarter results, which enables us to raise both our revenue and non-GAAP EPS guidance for the full year. We now expect revenue growth to be in the range from 9.5% to 10% in constant currency, and non-GAAP earnings per share in a range from $3.69 to $3.74. We believe that [COMPANY] is a stronger company today than it has ever been. We have invested tremendous effort over time to build scalable platforms, both operationally and financially, to enhance our relationships with clients and work with them to devise outsourcing solutions, which enable them to increase productivity and efficiency; to create a culture of continuous improvement in which our employees are open to working in new ways, which improve our efficiency and provide value to clients; and to maintain and enhance our scientific leadership. We have maintained our focus on early-stage drug research, strategically expanding our portfolio to provide clients with a critical capability they require to discover and develop new drugs. We have differentiated ourselves from the competition, and clients appreciate the value we bring to their research efforts, and the emphasis we place on individualized service. We are continuing with our outreach to heads of R&D and other decision-makers at the leading biopharmaceutical companies, as well as many of the larger biotech companies to ensure that they recognize our expanded product and service capabilities. All of these initiatives have positioned us exceptionally well to compete for business now, when global biopharma companies are making the decision to outsource. Biotech companies are investing in new funding in their pipeline, and academic institutions are working with biopharma companies to discover new drugs. We have been gaining market share, primarily due to the value of our portfolio and our scientific expertise, but also due to the fact that our competitors are in flux, with some in the process of changing hands, we have a unique opportunity to gain market share and we intend to capitalize on the opportunity. We had discussed our expectation for a better second half of the year, which was based primarily on the anniversary of the NCI contract cancellation and the reduction of a significant GEMS colony by one client. As anticipated, the Services businesses improved in the third quarter, resulting in revenue just slightly higher than in the third quarter of last year. Primarily as a result of sales to NCI researchers, Research Model revenue improved in North America, and we were very pleased to see a revenue increase in Europe as well. Sales in Japan continue to decline, but when looking at Asia in total, higher revenue in China more than offset the decline in Japan. China continues to present a significant opportunity for us, as the government and private industry both fund drug research. Therefore, we are expanding our footprint in China to increase our research model production and provide associated services. We are watching the market closely and intend to invest in broader capabilities as market demand requires. We continue to identify opportunities to streamline our RMS operations and we maintain our belief that an annual RMS operating margin in the high 20% range is achievable and sustainable. Organic revenue was also robust with both EMD and Biologics businesses delivering double-digit growth. The Biologics business performed very well in the third quarter, delivering strong revenue growth and an improved operating margin. We have invested, and will continue to invest in expanding our Biologics portfolio through the development of new assays and additional capabilities in order to provide a broader testing solution for our clients. The investment is particularly important now when the number of biologic drugs in development is increasing, as is demand for testing of biosimilars. Our goal is to be well-positioned to win market share in this expanding opportunity and we are pleased with the progress we have made to date. The legacy EMD business, again, reported growth above 10% as the PTS franchise continued to deliver strong sales. Our strategy to expand the capabilities of the PTS, including the MCS, and Nexus, has enabled EMD to increase revenue over time. We believe that the nextgen-PTS, which was recently launched at the PDA microconference in October, will continue to support EMD's growth. We believe our ability to provide a total microbial testing solution to our clients will be a key driver of our goal for the Microbial Solutions business to continue to deliver low double-digit organic revenue growth for the foreseeable future. The Manufacturing segment's operating margin improved by 40 basis points year-over-year to 33.4%, in line with our target in the low 30% range. Leverage from higher sales was significant, and efficiency initiatives undertaken in each of the segment's businesses also contributed to margin increase. The In Vivo Discovery business reported revenue growth over the prior year, driven primarily by oncology services. Our Early Discovery oncology franchise is benefiting from investment in oncology research, and also from market share gains. Our acquisitions of Argenta, BioFocus, and ChanTest have positioned [COMPANY] as a premier provider of early discovery services. As we anticipated in our acquisition plans, the strategies we are utilizing to increase client awareness of our broader portfolio are resulting in greater exposure for our Early Discovery businesses than they were able to gain as independent entities. We are continuing to hold discussions with numerous biopharma clients, and potential clients about playing a larger role in the discovery research efforts, and are optimistic that many of these companies will choose to outsource to us. We intend to play a leading role in this emerging opportunity, which we believe will be significant. We were exceptionally pleased to see the Safety Assessment business report another quarter of double-digit revenue growth over the third quarter last year and a 3.7% sequential increase. All of our facilities reported double-digit year-over-year revenue growth, resulting from improved client demand, a 5% increase in pricing, and market share gains. We are clearly taking market share across our client segments. We believe that when those decisions are made, [COMPANY] is the logical choice. Sales to biotech clients increased in double digits and were the primary driver of the revenue increase. As a whole, biotech companies have been the most consistent driver of our recent growth as they invested funding received from both the capital markets and from global biopharma, which is increasingly relying on biotech for drug discovery. As a result, for the last 2 years, biotech companies have represented a larger percentage of our revenue in global biopharma, and we expect that trend to continue. According to BioWorld, capital markets funding for biotech, which was already robust, strengthened in 2015. Biotech companies have discovered some of the most impactful drugs on the market and based on recent breakthroughs, it appears that they have identified promising new therapies for cancer, Alzheimer's and other complex diseases. Given the significant amount of funding raised by biotech companies over the last few years, we believe that even if the capital markets cool, the funds already in hand will support their growth for at least the next fiscal year and most probably beyond. Furthermore, we would not expect funding from global biopharma\r\n[Audio Gap]\r\ngoes to biotech, therefore, we expect that spending by biotech companies will continue to contribute to our revenue growth. As revenue has increased, our sustained focus on improving efficiency and productivity of the DSA business has led to significant operating margin expansion. Our segment margin increased 590 basis points in the third quarter to 24.2% from 18.3% last year, and 260 basis points sequentially. Now operating at near optimal capacity, we are opening additional study rooms in the fourth quarter, in Ohio, as planned, and looking forward to the first quarter next year when we expect to reopen Charles River Massachusetts. Situated less than an hour from the Boston-Cambridge biohub, perhaps the most significant concentration of medical research in the world, we believe that the Massachusetts facility is strategically located to support the demand for outsourced services and to accommodate hands-on research organizations, which want to be closely involved with a CRO partner. We are diligently marketing the facility, and have already received considerable indications of interest from large biopharma and emerging biotech companies, as well as academic research institutions. We believe it's particularly important that we continue to add capacity now when there is significant opportunity to gain market share. We have positioned [COMPANY] as the premier early-stage contract researcher organization, with a unique portfolio, and the scientific expertise to partner with all types of clients: Global biopharma clients, which are making a more significant commitment to outsourcing as they strive to improve operating efficiency and increase pipeline productivity; biotech companies, which have always preferred outsourcing to building infrastructure; and academic institutions, which are partnering with biopharma to monetize innovation and require partners to provide expertise in drug discovery and development. The outsourcing landscape has changed significantly over the last few years and now offers us many opportunities to work collaboratively with our clients. This is the reason that we continue to invest in portfolio expansion, scientific expertise, efficiency initiatives, and our people. These investments are the basis of our ability to provide a compelling value proposition to our clients. We intend to continue to identify and acquire businesses and technologies, primarily upstream, but also for other growth areas of our business. We believe that continued successful execution of our strategies will enable us to maintain and enhance our position as the leading pure play, early stage CRO, and allow [COMPANY] to provide value to clients, employees, and shareholders for the long term."]
