Name: 63_tobacco_vapor_cigarette_adult
Representative_Docs: ["Today, what I've got on the agenda to share with you -- the changes that are occurring amongst adult tobacco consumers in the market, how our operating companies are positioned to win in the combustible, smoke-free and vapor categories, and then lastly, I'm going to share with you our plan going forward for heat-not-burn technology, a technology whose time has finally arrived. The landscape continues to evolve quite dramatically. There are 3 consumer forces shaping the future of tobacco: first, the consumers move away from cigarettes, and we're seeing this in moist snuff, as well as vapor today; demographics, particularly the aging face of the U.S. consumer who's also becoming more multicultural; and the importance of value on the consumers' buying choices, not just price-led value, but real product and brand-led value. Understanding the whats and the whys of these changes, and developing innovative products is how we win the adult tobacco consumer, transform tobacco, and achieve our vision ultimately of market leadership. What is clear is that smoking and the adult smokers' desires have changed, and they will continue to evolve over time. But the question is, how might the demands of adult smokers and these changes reshape and transform the tobacco market? We've spent a considerable amount of time talking to adult smokers about what they'd like, what they want, and their ideal tobacco product compared to the products they use currently. What adult smokers tell us they want and desire in their ideal tobacco product, although is quite different than the products they currently consume. Far more smokers are interested in a vapor or aerosol-type product than is used today. And many more smokers are interested in switching to a smoke-free tobacco product than is currently consumed. What's obvious to me is what the consumers are saying versus actually what they're buying is the result of the fact that the vapor and smokeless products on the market today are not meeting their demands. What's needed are innovative, game-changing new products like VUSE, that truly have the potential to switch smokers and transform the tobacco category. Changing demographics are also reshaping the adult tobacco consumer. Ethnic segments, particularly Hispanics, will represent the vast majority of population growth over the coming decades. But ethnic diversity isn't the only important demographic trend having an impact on adult smokers. It's no joke, 50-plus is the new 30. The population is simply getting older and the baby-boomers are aging. The 50-plus demo is the fastest-growing segment, and in the not-too-distant future, will represent over half of all adult age cohort groups. Millennials will continue to gain the lion's share of press coverage, but the silvers will command the vast majority of wealth, spending power, and population. This is an important and changing demographic that we continue to pay close attention to in both our brands, as well as our innovations. And like changing demographics, it creates new growth opportunities for innovative brands and innovative products. Adult smokers are smoking less, but they're demanding a better, higher-quality smoking experience. They're demanding a better value, not necessarily a lower price, but a better smoking experience, and they're demanding stronger, more relevant, more energizing brands. With all these consumer forces at play, the imperatives to achieving our vision are clear. Our companies must achieve market leadership in all of the growth categories, particularly vapor and aerosol products, as well as smoke-free. They must develop superior innovations, not just generic technology, and must bring these innovations to market with speed. Our companies will continue to expand margin growth in cigarettes to invest in the growth of our brands and invest in transformative new innovations. And they must lead and shape reasonable and responsible regulation to ensure that these transformative categories can and will develop and that we will lead them. Now let's move to Camel, R.J. Reynolds' largest and fastest-growing brand, and the category's leading innovative premium brand. What continues to make Camel a winner is its innovative position in the marketplace, and its dynamic relationship with adult tobacco consumers. Camel, like its consumers, simply has a larger lust for life and a greater passion for its craft than your typical brand. Camel's market leading capsule range, the Crush Experience, is testament to Camel's craft and passion for innovation, and a real example of the broad appeal and the strength of the Camel equity. The growth and momentum in Camel's Crush Experience, and the increasing brand equity are accelerating Camel's growth amongst Hispanic adult smokers. The growing brand equity attributes, the increasing diversity of Camel's consumer base and innovation are what continues to elevate my confidence in Camel's growth potential. And we are investing in consumer-driven opportunities to expand the awareness of Pall Mall's product proposition and its brand proposition generally more. So clearly, growing awareness and growing trial are the key to accelerating good, solid, sustainable market share growth for Pall Mall into the future. The investments in Grizzly are paying off, and these investments continue to strengthen Grizzly's premium brand equities through innovative products and innovative marketing programs. The majority of what I'm going to talk about today are consumer and format trends given the difficulty and precisely determine the size and changes in the vapor category due to the extensive quantity of product launches, resulting in significant pipeline volume, the fact that reliable vapor shape -- vapor shop data is hard to access, as well as the rapid changes in formats. But what is very clear is the consumer interest in vapor continues to show a strong predictable pattern of growth. And they're consistent with what we saw last year, that consumer interest and usage are growing, and that consumers are not fully satisfied with the existing product offers, the main reason we don't see higher levels of usage and higher levels of volume in the market. Another key trend, we're seeing in the vapor category is the consumer moving away from disposables and into the tank liquid format. What we're seeing are distribution gains and consumers shopping around and searching for a vapor product that they can switch to. Generally speaking, if we think about this, the tanks are not very simple, convenient, or easy to use, and almost all cartridge products are not satisfying, don't taste good, and are unreliable. This tells us that quantity isn't what's important, but rather quality and satisfaction in a limited range of adult-oriented flavors will be what wins the day. Clearly, there's a lot right now that's changing in vapor.", "Altria delivered strong results and returns for our shareholders in 2012. Despite a continuing challenging external environment, our tobacco operating companies premium brands, Marlboro, Black & Mild, Copenhagen and Skoal had an excellent year as our companies continued investing in their long-term success. Altria grew its adjusted diluted earnings per share by 7.8% behind the business performance of our operating companies, complemented by higher earnings from our equity investment in SABMiller. Our employees' focus on our mission and values continues to drive our results. Our mission is to own and develop financially disciplined businesses that are leaders in responsibly providing adult tobacco and wine consumers with superior brand of products. We pursue our mission by focusing on 4 strategies: investing in leadership, aligning with society, satisfying adult consumers and creating substantial shareholder -- excuse me, creating substantial value for shareholders. Altria made significant progress in support of its mission in 2012 as we executed our core strategies and were guided by our values. Our first strategy, invest in leadership, reflects our focus on having excellent people and leading brands and external stakeholders important to our businesses' success. Our roughly 9,000 employees drive our company's success and we invest in programs to attract, develop, and retain talented and diverse employees. Our recruiting program, advancement planning process and leadership development programs provide our employees with skills and experiences to help them reach their full potential. Altria and its companies build relationships with business partners who promote actions consistent with our mission and values. Our companies work with a diverse base of suppliers, including minority and women-owned businesses. Our companies invest in the sustainability of their agricultural supply chains, which are critical to their business's success. Our success is tied to the communities where we live and work, and we invest our time and resources to support them. Altria has a long history of supporting the arts and continues to support organizations that bring world-class cultural experiences to our communities. In 2012, Altria ranked 30th on the Civic 50, which recognizes companies that best use their resources to improve their local communities and beyond. Our second strategy is to align with society by actively participating in resolving societal concerns that are relevant to our businesses. Significant progress has been made to reduce underage tobacco use. More work remains to be done, and our companies continue to contribute to this effort. Philip Morris USA, U.S. Smokeless Tobacco Company and John Middleton each develop and implement annual plans to help reduce underage tobacco use. They support responsible retailing through their trade programs and the We Card program, which provides resources to retailers to help them prevent tobacco sales to underage purchasers. These tobacco companies provided significant support for youth-serving organizations in 2012, combining their grant programs in education and positive youth development into 1 program we call Success360°. This initiative helps leading national and local nonprofit organizations effectively support middle school kids' academic achievement and healthy development, with a focus on helping them avoid risky behaviors like tobacco use. Our tobacco companies focus on complying with this law and constructively engaging with FDA and other stakeholders on issues related to the law. We have submitted comments to FDA covering a variety of important issues, met numerous times with FDA and presented to the Tobacco Products Scientific Advisory Committee. We will continue to engage and share science-based information with FDA and other stakeholders about regulatory issues important to our business. Our companies work to reduce their impact on the environment. After making significant progress against multiyear goals through 2012, we established new long-term goals to further reduce energy use and greenhouse gas emissions, implement sustainable water programs, increase recycling of waste from company facilities and to reduce the amount of material in product packaging. Our third strategy is to satisfy adult consumers by converting our deep understanding of adult tobacco and wine consumers into better and more creative products that satisfy their preferences. In 2012, PM USA introduced Marlboro's new architecture that focuses on the brands 4 product families: Red, Gold, Green and Black. The architecture allows PM USA to express Marlboro's essence and positioning in new ways, enabling the brand to expand its reach and breadth among adult smokers. Middleton has introduced new Black & Mild products that have helped the brand maintain its leadership position in the tipped cigarillo segment and expanded its presence in the growing untipped cigarillos segment. In recent years, Copenhagen maintained its leadership position in the natural segment and introduced or expanded products, including Copenhagen Long Cut Wintergreen, Long Cut Straight and Extra Long Cut Natural to broaden its product portfolio. Altria's tobacco companies have a deep understanding of adult tobacco consumers and work to develop products that meet their preferences. Adult tobacco consumers continue to express interest in tobacco alternatives. We are closely monitoring adult tobacco consumer interest in alternative products, and our companies are working internally and through partnerships to develop innovative new products for them. We believe that FDA regulation presents an opportunity relating to certain tobacco product innovation because the law expressly recognizes the potential role that modified risk tobacco products may play in reducing the harm caused by tobacco use. We have engaged with FDA extensively on this important topic, encouraging the agency to develop scientific standards that are rigorous yet feasible for evaluating potentially less hazardous products. Our fourth strategy is to create substantial value for shareholders. In the smokeable products segment, PM USA and Middleton's strategy is to maximize income while maintaining modest share momentum over time on Marlboro and Black & Mild. Our companies remain focused on managing cost structures. Altria took a number of steps in the last year to help maintain its balance sheet strength. Altria's strong balance sheet supports our ability to return cash to shareholders, primarily in the form of dividends. Altria joined with a broad coalition of businesses, associations and shareholders to support making permanent the lower personal tax rates on dividend income and maintaining parity between the tax treatment of dividends and capital of gains. Altria also has repurchased stock when we have concluded that it is the best use of cash to maximize shareholder value. In 2012, we continued to achieve success in managing litigation, although we continue to face substantial challenges, as we have for many years. Altria's pursuit of its mission has supported the consistent delivery of solid annual adjusted EPS growth and excellent total returns to its shareholders. Our consistent adjusted diluted EPS growth and strong and growing dividend supported total shareholder returns that have exceeded the returns of the broader market and similar companies. A number of organizations have recognized our strong performance in pursuit of our mission. We're pleased with our business performance and we're proud of the results we've achieved. We believe that our executive compensation programs are an important contributor to them and to our strong shareholder returns. These programs are designed to align the interest of executives and shareholders to promote the company's mission and business strategies and to reward the achievement of corporate and individual performance goals.", "2019 was a dynamic year for the tobacco category. For [PERSON], it was a year characterized by 2 distinct stories: the outstanding performance of [PERSON]'s core tobacco businesses and significant progress advancing our noncombustible business platform alongside disappointing performance from our JUUL investment. Across our businesses, our employees accomplished more with less and responsibly delivered outstanding results. Despite unexpected challenges with our investment in JUUL, which led to impairment charges and reported losses, we grew adjusted diluted earnings per share by 5.8% and continue to reward our shareholders with growing cash dividends. Our core tobacco businesses delivered strong financial performance, with each of the smokeable and smokeless product segments delivering high single-digit adjusted operating companies income growth, significantly expanding their adjusted operating companies income margins and maintaining strength on their leading premium brands. In fact, if you look at the performance of our smokeable and smokeless products segments on a combined basis over the past 5 years, 2019 was a high watermark for combined adjusted OCI and margin expansion. In addition, we exceeded our $575 million cost reduction target, made significant progress advancing and building our noncombustible business platform with the launch of IQOS in 2 lead markets and the completion of the on! And we successfully advocated for moving the legal age to purchase all tobacco products to 21 to address social access concerns among youth. We are disappointed in the performance of our JUUL investment in 2019, and we recorded a second impairment of the JUUL investment, which Billy will discuss in more detail shortly. It's a critical time for the e-vapor category, and we believe manufacturers must take responsible steps in the short-term to protect the long-term opportunity that the category presents for adult smokers looking for alternatives. We believe that the e-vapor category in its current form needs a reset, and we believe the most important next steps to create a sustainable path forward are FDA's review and ultimate decisions on PMTA filings and driving down youth usage of e-vapor. We believe the new board structure will provide diverse perspectives and independent expertise to help JUUL's management team successfully and responsibly navigate the very dynamic e-vapor market going forward. For [PERSON], we remain committed to preventing kids and non-tobacco users from using tobacco products. Although this is significant progress, we're troubled by the alarming rise in youth e-vapor use. This is why in early 2019, we launched a national campaign to raise the minimum tobacco purchase age to 21 and worked persistently with state and federal lawmakers to support this legislation. We have much more work ahead of us in reversing the youth e-vapor trends, and our efforts will not stop at Tobacco 21. We must continue to advance harm reduction. There are approximately 40 million adult smokers in the U.S. today, with more than half interested in alternative products. While JUUL forges its way in an ever-changing e-vapor category, we remain highly focused on our portfolio approach with alternative products like IQOS and on!. We want our organization, including our sales force, to most effectively and responsibly advance the noncombustible portfolio options we're building, and we're moving forward on these opportunities responsibly and with increased resources. With IQOS, we're encouraged by early interest from adult smokers and excitement from the trade. Philip Morris International's MRTP application for IQOS remains pending with the FDA, and we remain optimistic about its authorization. We plan to capitalize on our first-mover advantage while considering the opportunities presented by an FDA-authorized reduced risk claim for IQOS 2.4 and the launch of a more modern device. In oral nicotine pouches, we're advancing our plans quickly in this rapidly growing category, focusing on regulatory, manufacturing and distribution efforts. As e-vapor goes through a period of transition, we believe it's an opportune time to further invest in our plans in heated tobacco and oral nicotine. The strength of our core tobacco businesses provides us with the financial flexibility to make these investments as we capitalize on our first-mover advantage in heated tobacco and on! We enter 2020 with continued focus on harm reduction and preparing for a future where adult tobacco consumers overwhelmingly prefer noncombustible products over combustible products. For our JUUL investment, we now expect HSR resolution in the first half of 2020. Therefore, we've lowered our 2020 through 2022 compounded annual adjusted diluted EPS earnings growth objective to 4% to 7% from our previously announced objective of 5% to 8%."]

Name: 64_recession_stimulus_economy_consumer
Representative_Docs: ["So there was a big -- the reason it's flattish is because of the whole stimulus. There was a huge wave that came in through the stimulus to us. We saw this big bump due to the stimulus, but also unemployment. And then we saw another even increased bump in July, and that was due, it looked like, to the economy opening up again, the tax -- fact that taxes were delayed and the end of the stimulus funds that were in our major programs. And so you're comparing 2 quarters where there was this huge governmental and very extraordinary situation to this quarter. But what we're seeing now is continued year-over-year growth in the mid-30s. If we do get another stimulus, the same thing will happen. So it will be hard to really decipher, but it will be over our current growth rate, which is in the 30s already. There is sustainable -- 20% to 30% GDV growth at the minimum in that portfolio going into the next, we think, a couple of years. We think it's going to be high-growth for a while.", "The market is really off to a rough start. Just to summarize my approach to this, the definition of a surprise is an event that I believe has a better than 50% chance of taking place, where the average investor would give it no better than a 1 out of 3 chance. So it's a little below the norm, but I've found that there is more information content sometimes in the ones I get wrong than the ones I get right. My thinking was that the economy was going to be growing faster than it turned out to grow. There's no question that cyber hackers, terrorists have gotten into both government systems and corporate systems. But basically, cyber attacks have risen to an important part of the awareness of both corporate and government life. I thought the market would be up 15% and as we all painfully know, it was only flat for 2015. So it was a very rough year, and as you'll see in the Surprises of 2016, I expect 2016 to be a rough year too. [PERSON] became concerned that the European economy was slipping back into recession and agreed to do whatever it takes and pump money into the European economy as vigorously as he possibly could, and I think it's working. I think Europe will grow between 1% and 2% in 2016. It turned out to be up in both, but the [PERSON] program, which was designed to put Japan on a sustained growth path really didn't work as effectively as many people had hoped. But clearly, China is slowing down. But service jobs don't pay as much as manufacturing jobs and their exports are down. So as you'll see in the Surprises of 2016, I don't think they're growing anywhere near 7% but they'll probably report someplace between 6% and 7%. The Iran deal is signed. There was even controversy when it was signed. And now, we have a further problem because of the conflict between Iran and Saudi Arabia. I thought there would be some opportunities in the high-yield sector because of the distressed debt was -- had been beaten down badly. I think the American voting public is dissatisfied with the ineffectiveness of Congress. And I thought that, that would -- the Republicans would try to seize that opportunity and show that they could get legislation passed. Now that [PERSON] has taken over as Speaker of the House, there's been some progress made. He has gotten a budget bill through, and I think he is trying to reposition the party as a can do party. They will be summarized in the Ten Surprises, but the first thing is I think the Fed is in a tightening mode and you shouldn't fight the Fed. Second, there is a general agreement among strategists that the S&P 500 is going to be up 10% in 2016. I don't think the factors are in place for the market to do that well and we're certainly off to a bad start. Three, wages are increasing and companies don't have much pricing power. So profit margins, which are near an all-time high, have to be squeezed and that's obviously going to have an impact on the way investors perceive equities. So I think we're going to be in another year of disappointing earnings. The high-yield market is in disarray. The consensus estimate for world growth is 3%. I think the U.S. could grow at less than 2% and I think world growth could be ratcheted down to something like 2%. So I think it's going to be a tough year for growth around the world. And finally, fear of terrorism is dampening consumer confidence. And so I think that's going to affect the economy. So I think we're in for a rough year even though it's an election year in 2016. Well, it's election year and you have to make a judgment. I think [PERSON] is going to win the election. The Democrats have a leg up in the electoral college. I think [PERSON] will be the candidate. But I think the confluence of factors here indicate that the market is going to be down. I know January so far has been a very difficult beginning, but my view is the year will be down. But I don't think stocks are going to be up in 2016. I don't think they'll do that, and the reason is that they say they are data dependent. The economy won't be growing fast enough for them to feel comfortable raising rates 4 times this year. The fourth one is that the world economy is softer than people think and that the dollar appreciates -- I mean, depreciates. What we have here is a weak American economy and that it gets reflected in the currency. Even though the European economy won't be robust, I think the European economy relative to what people think is going to be better than expected. The U.S. economy is going to be worse. On China, I still think they're going to avoid a hard landing, but I think things are very tough in China. Almost all the figures I look at on the manufacturing side indicates that China is going to be very slow, maybe 5% or less. The service sector is growing, but people are paid less there. But overall, I think the economy isn't going to grow at 7% or even 6%. Number six. And my thinking is that the European Union isn't going to break up. And I think with the strains of the refugee crisis, there's going to be much more talk about the European Union breaking up and going back to the national currencies. Oil will languish in the $30s. There are heavy inventories, production is still continuing, demand is diminishing and Iran is going to be able to ship oil in international markets. I think we're going to see oil stay in the $30s, may have blips up into the $40s, but basically, it's going to be consolidating at present levels. A lot of buildings are being built, a lot of houses in London are for sale at very fancy prices, and I think there's going to be a severe correction in the residential market. I don't think this is going to be true in the commercial market, but I think high-end residential in New York and London is going to suffer a setback. Soft U.S. economy and a soft equity market causes the 10-year treasury to trade consistently below 2.5%. The third most crowded trade is everybody believes that the 10-year treasury is going to have a 3% coupon by year-end, that yields are going to go up. I think -- and not only that, but I think investors are seeking liquidity, and so I think you're going to see the yield on the 10-year stay below 2.5%. And finally, burdened by heavy debt and slower global growth, world growth stays at 2% -- comes down to 2%, not the 3% that everybody expects. Okay, there are the ten surprises. I think investors are beginning to get a little impatient with the fact that the companies are using financial engineering to substitute for growth, that they're using share buybacks and mergers and acquisitions because they don't see the revenue increases that would allow them to have higher earnings per share. And I think that they were on the brink of breakthroughs in heart disease, cancer, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, diabetes, and I think that's going to be some of the good news of 2016. And finally, I would love to be bullish on the emerging markets, and at some point, I will be, but 2016 is not the year. I think investors are too pessimistic about equities. This shows that pension funds are too optimistic about returns. So my view is that pension funds and endowments are going to have to trim their sites and be more modest in their objectives, and they're going to have to construct their portfolios for lower expectations. The Fed increased its balance sheet from $1 trillion to $4.5 trillion since 2008, and they're not paying any of those bonds. The point is that the stock markets around the world and the economies around the world have been heavily dependent on monetary stimulus for growth. And this year, I don't think the earnings are going to be there to support it and that's why I have a negative stance. This shows that it's best to be in equities when the Fed is easing and when the Fed is not accommodative, the market usually has a difficult time and the Fed has moved to a more restrictive monetary policy. So this has been a period where corporations have benefited at the expense of workers and so profit margins are at an all-time high, and I'm not convinced that they can stay at these levels. If you're trying to forecast the price of oil, the best thing to do is look at what world growth is. There is a high correlation between world growth, which has come down from 3.6% down to 3% and the price of oil has come down with it. And that's certainly been a factor, but it's really the slowdown of world growth that has been the principal cause of the decline in the price of oil. Looking at the U.S. economy. We've been growing at 2% to 3%, and I think this year is going to be closer to 2%. Manufacturing is below 50% on the ISM reading and services are being pretty close to 60%, so the economy is being held up by service sector strength, not manufacturing. You can see revenues. So revenues are very modest and that's been the problem for earnings. And I think this is the inequality issue, the fact that the middle class doesn't feel they're making any gains is going to be very important an election issue. And this is going to be a very important social and political issue going forward, not just this year, but going forward. The consumer is saving more because of his or her anxiety about the outlook, and I expect that to continue. The unemployment, we're all celebrating the fact that we've gotten unemployment from 10% down to 5%, but if you adjust the unemployment for the decline in the participation rate, it's a different story. Now some of those are legitimate retirees from the baby boom era, but some of them are people who have been so frustrated looking for a job that they've given up on it. It's certainly not the Democrats, but, in fact, our unemployment rate is higher than the reported number. They are buying necessities and perhaps a few luxuries, but basically, the consumer is holding back. Now with unit labor costs going up around 2% and 2.5%, productivity has come down to below 1%. And so, therefore, we can expect stagnant standards of living going forward. We're back up into a layoff mode where companies are continuing to try to provide -- buy capital equipment that allows them to get the goods and services out the door with fewer workers. There are 2 parts of the economy that are favorable. And as favorable as we like it, housing is favorable where over 1 million starts, and the people in the 25 to 34 age group are finding jobs and they're willing to get married, form families, move into their own home. I think the consumer will do okay, but there won't be a consumer spending boom. This shows that the rig count is down, and so at some future point, with the depletion of wells and the increase of demand, we're going to have a supply-demand constraint and the price of oil is going to go up, but that's not going to happen in 2016. Just take a look at the European economy. It's projected to grow between 1% and 2%. So the economic health of Europe is probably better than most of you perceive. They have substantial reserves and they're willing to use them to stimulate the economy. So I think China is slowing, but I still think it's going to grow faster than almost -- than any developed economy. This shows that China consumes generally between 1/3 and 1/2 of all industrial economies and the fact that China's growth is slowing down is one of the reasons the emerging markets are suffering recessions. There are a number of companies that are showing earnings improvements in Japan and the price earnings ratio of Japan is below that of Europe and the United States.", "First of all, I'm not sure we're going to have a recession. Secondly, I have no idea if we have a recession, how deep or extended it will be? I'm not sure even what the definition of  the recession is anymore. Because we got this committee deciding whether we're in a recession or not, and they usually declare it a couple of quarters after it happens."]

Name: 65_ethanol_carbon_diesel_renewable
KeyBERT: ['renewable diesel', 'renewable fuels', 'renewable fuel', 'biodiesel', 'sustainable aviation', 'biofuels', 'biogas', 'low carbon', 'aviation fuel', 'biofuel']
Representative_Docs: ["Let's discuss our Carbon Zero sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel project in Riverbank, California. In December 2021, after 3 years of negotiations with the City of Riverbank and the U.S. Army, Aemetis signed the acquisition of the 125-acre Riverbank Industrial Complex under a sale and lease agreement. Earlier this year, [PERSON] took operational control of the Riverbank site for construction of our sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel plant as well as the construction of the Riverbank portion of our CO2 sequestration well project. We have signed and announced more than $3.8 billion of sales contracts with Delta Airlines, American Airlines, Japan Airlines, Qantas and other airlines. Incentives included in the pending federal legislation, I should say, that now past federal legislation, expand the market for sustainable aviation fuel by allowing a price to airlines that is competitive with petroleum jet fuel. In addition, we signed a $3.2 billion renewable diesel sales agreement to deliver 45 million gallons per year under a 10-year sales contract with a major travel stop chain for its Northern California locations. In October 2020, the Aemetis ethanol plant in California was identified in the study issued by the Stanford University Center for carbon capture as 1 of 3 ethanol plant CO2 sources in California that have the highest potential return on investment from building a carbon capture and sequestration facility, compared to the oil refineries, cement plants and natural gas power plants that comprise the 61 largest CO2 emission sources in California. In Phase 1 of [COMPANY] project, we plan to inject up to 400,000 metric tons per year of CO2 emissions from our biogas, ethanol and jet diesel plants into 2 sequestration wells, which we plan to drill near our 2 biofuels plant sites in California. In summary, Aemetis is expanding a diversified portfolio of negative carbon intensity projects, dairy renewable natural gas, biodiesel in India, sustainable aviation and renewable diesel fuel, low-carbon ethanol using zero carbon intensity electricity, renewable hydrogen and CO2 sequestration. All of these projects are synergistic and create what we refer to as a circular bioeconomy within Aemetis in which we use byproducts and waste products of our own facilities and local areas as feedstock to produce low and negative carbon intensity renewable fuels.", "Aemetis was founded in 2006 and now have 4 lines of business focused on supplying low carbon and below-zero carbon renewable fuels and biochemicals. Included in our production portfolio is a 60 million gallon per year capacity ethanol, distillers grain and corn oil plant located in Keyes, California, near Modesto. To support our carbon reduction efforts that decrease our costs and increase the value of our biofuels, we have been awarded about $21 million of grants this year to support energy efficiency and other upgrades to our California ethanol plant. In keeping with our focus of providing value-added solutions to our customers, this plan will build on our foundation of delivering high-margin products, software and services that help petitioners drive more successful, more profitable businesses while providing the best-in-quality care. As part of our ongoing efforts to advance our leadership position in the dental equipment and specialty dental -- specifically the digital dentistry, we are pleased to announce that we entered into a 3-year agreement with Dentsply Sirona effective September 1, 2017, to distribute Dentsply Sirona's full line of dental equipment in the United States. Also, relative to our Dental business, as mentioned on our earnings call -- our last earnings call and of course, in the press releases that we've issued, we recently closed on the acquisition of Southern Anesthesia + Surgical, or SAS as commonly known in the marketplace, which offers surgical supplies and pharmaceuticals to approximately 11,500 oral surgeons, dentists and of course, dental anesthesiologists and periodontists across the U.S. SAS had 2016 sales of $72 million and will be an excellent addition to our product offering targeting the needs of dental surgeons. This reflects particularly strong patient traffic to physician offices, particularly related to the late flu season, as well as our continued execution in serving the market, as it is consolidating among large group practices, including the integrated delivery network. We are well-positioned to help primary care practices and ambulatory surgical centers operate efficiently so our customers can focus on patient outcomes. We believe that promoting wellness and prevention is key to the future of improving the health care landscape. In line with helping physicians provide better clinical care, we recently announced an exclusive distribution agreement with Rijuven to sell its CardioSleeve diagnostic device to medical practitioners. CardioSleeve is the world's first stethoscope attachment that provides electrocardiogram and heart data via Bluetooth for instant analysis, another reflection of the digitalization of health care, an area that we are highly committed to advancing. This product is an excellent example of our expansion of innovative medical devices in our portfolio that we are helping doctors provide effective treatment and more efficient care. Again, very pleased, not only with our Dental and Animal Health performance, but on the Medical side as well. And of course, enhancing our technology solutions offering is an important initiative as we empower our customers to do more with the tools we provide them to help boost productivity and yes, improve efficiency in the practice."]

Name: 73_depression_sage_ppd_217
Representative_Docs: ["We've had a productive and eventful last few months at [COMPANY] as we continue our transformation from developing a single compound in a single indication to a company that's advancing multiple compounds in multiple clinical stage trials. We remain focused on creating an industry-leading pipeline of medicines, leveraging the extrasynaptic GABA mechanism of action, and we are beginning to see these efforts come to fruition. And we're now beginning to explore our pipeline's utility in much larger indications. Based on our recent positive results in our SAGE-547 study of postpartum depression, or PPD, we've expanded our Phase II development program exploring SAGE-547 for PPD with the initiation of 2 clinical trials in moderate and severe PPD, and we've already enrolled our first patient in this program. With respect to SAGE-217, we now plan to focus initial development on essential tremor and postpartum depression, with Phase II studies set to begin this year in both. As we consider other new indications for SAGE-217, we'll continue to exploit small, efficient, proof-of-concept studies to guide our portfolio strategy. We, therefore, plan to begin 2 small proof-of-concept studies in Parkinson's disease using SAGE-217 and in Major Depressive Disorder using SAGE-547 to further study the application of this mechanism and to guide the expansion of our pipeline. Further, we're also evaluating several additional candidates within our GABA pipeline, such as SAGE-105 and SAGE-324, to explore their potential impact in such GABA-related CNS disorders as orphan epilepsies. But we have identified a number of needed clarifications to guide screening of patients to prevent overexclusion of patients who may benefit from therapy. And we're confident that our updates and clarification to the inclusion and exclusion criteria will bring us in line with our enrollment model and will allow us to report data in the first half of next year. More broadly, based on our recent positive trial readout and the potential opportunities before us, we are currently undertaking a full portfolio review of our GABA-based candidates as well as expanding our research efforts to identify additional indications with a biological rationale for treatment that accompanies differentiated GABA compounds. This effort will extend research into other mood and affective disorders, such as depression, panic and mania, as well as other neurological disorders. In closing, we believe our recent clinical data are both promising and potentially transformative for both Sage and the CNS patients that we serve. It gives us near-term opportunities in several indications with both SAGE-547 and SAGE-217, while also opening the door for a broader GABA-based development effort into other movement, mood and affective disorders. We remain focused on executing on the opportunities before us, and we'll continue to appropriately balance our resources across our growing portfolio as we continue to expand.", "We believe that SAGE is pursuing a unique, data-driven approach to CNS drug development, by employing efficient human proof-of-concept studies, not only to uncover activity signals, but also to guide the design of future clinical trials before investing in larger programs. In this study, we sought to understand safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and activity of SAGE 217 in the cohort of 12 open label Parkinson's patients in order to determine whether there is a suitable activity signal to justify further development and if so, to help develop the methodology needed to expedite progress into more formal Phase II testing. The design allowed us to examine which symptoms were responsive to levodopa/carbidopa, which were responsive to SAGE-217's mechanism of action, and if they were any responses unique to 217 worthy of continued investigation. In this trial we observed that levodopa/carbidopa activity was primarily focused on the motor symptoms of bradykinesia and rigidity. By contrast, SAGE 217 activity was primarily focused on tremor symptoms. In this population of Parkinson's disease patients, administration of SAGE 217 during the day was found to be generally well tolerated with no SAEs or discontinuations. We believe these data justify proceeding to an additional open label Part B study. We plan to evaluate SAGE 217 as an adjunctive treatment to anti-Parkinsonian agents. We are seeking to confirm this activity signal in an adjunctive crossover design prior to designing a formal placebo-controlled Phase II program. Based on the findings we've described, the patient population for the next trial cohort will be targeted now to patients with tremor-predominant symptoms. We're also interested in further evaluating non-motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease, including depression, anxiety, cognition and sleep. We also announced today that we've initiated dosing of SAGE 217 in the Phase II Part B, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in Major Depressive Disorder following the positive open-label Part A data. The Part B study is evaluating moderate-to-severe Major Depressive Disorder patients with baseline HAM-D total scores of 22 or greater. We expect this study to involve eight sites in the United States, along with safety and tolerability of the [ EMA ] Part B, is to determine if treatment with SAGE 217 improves depressive symptoms in patients compared to placebo. SAGE 718 is a novel oral, first-in-class, oxysterol-based, positive allosteric modulator of the NMDA receptor. Positive modulation of NMDA receptors may have potential in the treatment of a range of neurologic disorders associated with a variety of cognitive, neurologic and behavioral symptoms. On the GABAA receptor modulation side of our portfolio, we are pleased to announce that we've selected SAGE 324 as our next novel oral development candidate, intended to be developed through the focus on indications involving GABA hypofunction, including epilepsy. Many of our studies are first of their kind and takes a tremendous level of perseverance and commitment to bring new potential therapies to those who need the most.", "So one of the things I neglected to say is I am a psychiatrist by training, and so as much as I gave the disclaimer that we don't choose sides, this has been equally as exciting for me as it has for [PERSON]. SAGE-217 represents our first oral molecule in development. And one of the things that we've been doing, and I touched upon it briefly before, is we look to see, as we do our development -- and the next slide, [PERSON] -- we try to make sure that as we move forward into clinical development, we're building on information that we've already obtained. The development program that we've announced for SAGE-217 is focused on 2 key areas: it's mood disorders and movement disorders. We've had placebo-controlled data with SAGE-547 in both postpartum depression, as [PERSON] so eloquently described, as well as in movement disorders with essential tremor data that has been presented at the American Academy of Neurology and that [PERSON] shared with you earlier today. The development program, however, for 217, is attempting to build on that. So we already feel like from a mechanistic standpoint, we understand how to measure postpartum depression as well as essential tremor. So we'll be moving 217 into both postpartum depression, but also into major depressive disorder. [PERSON] did give us our rationale already about why that might be important. There's a connection, not only with allopregnanolone in postpartum depression but potentially all the way through the Major Depression itself. For essential tremor, we've seen placebo-controlled data, and we believe that the risks going directly into a placebo-controlled trial with SAGE-217 in that area as well as lead to highly leveraged opportunities in other movement disorders, and in this case we've selected for the initial clinical trial Parkinson's disease, which I believe, was at today, we announced we just began dosing. Even as we design our Phase I program, we want to make sure that the kind of innovation, kind of questions that [PERSON] and [PERSON] are asking are addressable inside of that program. But our intent, of course, is to inform development of other compounds in the -- in our pipeline as well as to derisk how we're going to go about doing clinical trials subsequently. So in our program, not only did we do the basics, of course, but we've really added in some bits of information that we think are really going to jump-start our ability to move forward with 217 into early Phase II and to subsequent Phase II trials. Really important way that make use of both the nonclinical data as well as our clinical data, something that we will continue to do as we progress both 217 as well as other compounds in this series. Why postpartum depression? As I said, we will be doing 4 Phase II trials with SAGE-217: postpartum depression, major depressive disorder, essential tremor and Parkinson's. I don't need to belabor the point, we really do believe that allopregnanolone provides a reasonable model. Of course, a very, a robust data that we saw on the Phase II trial makes us have a lot of confidence with the mechanism that we're touching on really is a unique one and a potentially a very powerful one for these patients. But we do think that an oral molecule represent a unique form for a novel -- a new chemical entity and one that we think is going to be very important moving forward for postpartum depression. Because we understand the pharmacology and the way in which SAGE-217 hits our extrasynaptic GABA receptors, we do believe that there is a very high likelihood of read-through between 547 and 217. This is a program that we'll be progressing very rapidly into a placebo-controlled study. Why essential tremor? But many of you know, as we've talked about it over time, there's a fundamental relationship between a GABA in the cerebellum and the GABA disruption in -- looks like to be the pathophysiology of essential tremor itself. In the case of essential tremor, we're proceeding with a very -- what we think is a novel trial design. So it's a very powerful way to get a lot of information not only about whether the drug works, whether it persists at working, but also what the optimal dosing strategy might be in these patients. Why Parkinson's disease? [PERSON] and [PERSON] both laid out why we think we might actually have some activity there. Parkinson's, we often think of it as a disorder of dopamine. Parkinson's affects mood. Many of the disorders that we've talked about that might have either a GABA or glutamate mechanism, are present in patients that have Parkinson's disease, both from the earliest stages in some of those movement disorders and some of these other non -- the sort of non-severe forms of Parkinson's. Again, like what we're doing for major depressive disorder, we are not going to do this in an unmindful way. Assuming that we have positive signal, we would rapidly move into a placebo-controlled trial as well. So the pattern that we intend to do for our development is to replicate first the -- an open-label, look at the best way to treat patients, and then move into a placebo-controlled in ways -- a placebo trial in ways that allow us to really understand the best patients, the best way to treat them, so that when we get data at the far end of all of this work, we know what to make of it. So 217, and I'll finish on this note, we are well positioned to development in broad markets. There's a lot of opportunity. And we've identified 2 main themes that we're pursuing at least through 2017: the mood and movement. And there'll be a very steady flow over the first half into the second half of the year for this very coordinated Phase II program around 217."]
